mn136:5.3: The four ways of answering a question are: directly, after analysing it, with a counter-question, or by setting it aside (replying with silence). Here the question required an answer after analysis.
mn136:6.3: This is a quotation of the Buddha’s own words elsewhere (cf. Sutta 38 and the Saḷāyatanavagga of the Saṁyutta Nikāya).
mn136:8.3: This is the list of the ten unprofitable courses of kamma; see Sutta 41.
mn136:8.7: This is the list of the ten profitable courses of kamma; see Sutta 41.
mn136:9.1: Devadatta is a well-known example of this first case: he persuaded Prince Ajātasattu to murder his father (a Stream-winner), thrice attempted to murder the Buddha, wounding him once, and caused a schism in the Saṅgha—the last two acts alone being certain to lead to rebirth in hell.
mn136:17.2: This threefold list appears to mean: ‘earlier’—either earlier in that life, before the good or evil courses of kamma described were undertaken, or in some previous life; ‘later’—later in that same life, since even one who does much evil kamma will usually also do some good occasionally; and ‘at the time of death’—referring to a deathbed wrong view of the type ‘there is no kamma, no result of kamma, no evil, no result of evil’, since the next birth depends on the object occupying a dying person’s mind in the last moments.
mn136:18.1: A well-known example is the story of ‘Copper-tooth’, the public executioner who, after a career of murder as a bandit and then fifty years as an executioner, was taught by the venerable Sāriputta and, his mind eased of the weight of evil kamma, attained a heavenly rebirth. See the Dhammapada Commentary, ii, 203–209.
mn136:19.1: King Pasenadi of Kosala is a well-known example of this case.
mn136:20.1: This was what happened to Queen Mallikā, wife of King Pasenadi: though she led a good life, generous and virtuous, she once had sexual relations with a dog; this unconfessed evil weighed on her mind and came to her at the time of death, causing seven days in hell, after which the power of her many good kammas gave her a heavenly rebirth. See the Dhammapada Commentary, iii, 119–123.
mn136:21.1: The Commentary explains these four terse cases: (1) a strong unprofitable kamma whose result comes before that of weaker unprofitable kammas; (2) a profitable kamma followed by an unprofitable death-proximate kamma which makes the former incapable of yielding its result immediately; (3) a strong profitable kamma that fruits even before much accumulated unprofitable kamma; (4) an unprofitable kamma followed by a profitable death-proximate kamma which fruits first and yields a good result.
